bridges.mechanism: An increase in Russian operational tempo accelerates battlefield use, production and refinement of long‑range strike systems (notably drones and cruise missiles) and associated tactics that are then proliferated or emulated by Iran and its proxies, enabling higher frequency and scale of missile/drone attacks in the Gulf.

Rises in cross‑border kinetic strikes tend to be accompanied by retaliatory or preemptive offensive cyber operations against command, control and critical systems (including AI infrastructure), increasing the observed frequency of successful cyberattacks.

Repeated cross-border strikes on ships, ports and routes raise insurance and freight premiums and trigger route suspensions, creating an immediate market risk premium that pushes up refined fuel prices.

A rise in cross‑border strikes increases expectations on third parties to take clear positions or impose constraints; visible ambiguity or non‑cooperation from Beijing in the face of such incidents erodes U.S. perceptions of reliability and lowers bilateral strategic trust.

Damage and outages to energy production and transmission degrade data‑center uptime and edge connectivity in affected areas, directly slowing the rate at which new or updated AI models and services can be deployed and scaled.
Kinetic damage, power loss or operational interruptions at refineries and associated utilities directly reduces processing capacity and forces shutdowns or lower runs.
Physical attacks or sabotage to pipeline segments, pumping stations and terminals force immediate pump-stops and route closures, cutting volumes transiting the network.

Disruption to Russian/European energy infrastructure shifts crude and refined product flows onto Middle Eastern suppliers, increasing tanker transits and chokepoint traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and thereby raising congestion, insurance/escorting requirements and the incidence of maritime trade interruptions in the Gulf.

Widespread outages and damage to energy supply and transport infrastructure reduce output and processing capacity at mines/refineries and raise shipping/insurance costs, directly lowering the volume of critical‑mineral shipments flowing through the bilateral corridor.

Tighter export controls and trade restrictions reduce sanctioned actors' access to advanced accelerators, cloud compute and specialized software, directly constraining their ability to train and operate large, high‑performance models and lowering their model capability level within the affected jurisdictions.
Expanded sanctions and trade controls block buyers, restrict shipping/insurance and freeze related logistics and payments, directly preventing affected producers from loading and exporting crude.

A sharp escalation in sanctions and trade restrictions tied to the Russia–Ukraine war polarizes international diplomacy, consumes diplomatic bandwidth and sidelines neutral mediation channels, reducing the frequency and substantive depth of diplomatic engagement aimed at de‑escalating Iran–Gulf tensions.

Expansion and tightening of sanctions regimes produce new legal authorities, compliance regimes and precedent that governments and regulators quickly extend to broader export-control rules on sensitive technologies (to close re‑export loopholes and prevent sanctioned actors from acquiring dual‑use items).

Stronger operational and intelligence coordination among allies produces joint requirements, pooled funding and shared standards for defensible AI in military use, prompting immediate increases in coordinated safety engineering projects and resource allocation.

Stronger allied operational coordination and deployments to support Ukraine reallocate Western naval and air assets to Europe, reducing available forces and political willingness to conduct or scale high‑intensity military responses in the Gulf, thereby lowering state response intensity.

Stronger operational and policy coordination among allies leads to harmonized procurement standards, joint restriction lists and aligned certification requirements that force suppliers to split product lines and supply chains, increasing technological ecosystem fragmentation.

Increased missile/drone strikes provoke and coincide with retaliatory and preemptive offensive cyber operations that include targeting adversary AI infrastructure, raising the rate of successful cyberattacks on AI systems.

A sharp uptick in missile/drone strikes in the Gulf forces divergent threat prioritization and political calculations among the US and European allies, producing public disagreements over force posture and burden‑sharing that weaken operational and policy coordination toward Ukraine.

Escalated state military operations create urgent requirements for reliable, hardened AI capabilities, prompting defense budgets and acquisition programs to allocate more resources to safety, robustness testing and hardening projects.

State strikes, seizures or security operations targeting pipeline corridors, pumping stations or access roads force temporary shutdowns or reduced operating capacity, lowering transit volumes through pipelines.

Intensified state military responses by the US and partners in the Gulf consume precision munitions, ISR and logistics capacity and prompt temporary reallocation of shipments and stocks that delays or reduces deliveries of long‑range strike and air‑defense systems to Ukraine, degrading Kyiv's ability to blunt Russian offensives and enabling higher Russian operational tempo.

Interruptions and rerouting of shipping delay or block delivery of high‑end GPUs, cooling systems and other datacenter hardware, directly reducing available training capacity and thus achievable model capability in the near term.
Physical interdiction of tankers, attacks on ports/terminals and the imposition of de facto no-go zones prevent crude cargoes from loading or reaching export routes, directly reducing export volumes.

Increased interdiction and rerouting raise freight costs, insurance premiums and delivery times for refined products and marine bunkers, producing an immediate risk/freight-driven uplift in spot fuel prices.

Attacks and interdictions in the Gulf raise insurance, force ship diversions and port delays, directly reducing the volume and frequency of critical-mineral shipments traversing the US–China shipping corridor.

Visible disruption to sea lines of communication prompts security agencies and regulators to tighten export licensing and controls on sensitive technologies to limit supply-chain vulnerabilities and perceived leakage risks.
Sustained, high-intensity diplomatic contacts and de-escalatory signaling reduce market risk premia and insurance/freight surcharges, exerting downward pressure on spot fuel prices.

Greater policy alignment among allied states leads to coordinated export controls, shared standards and joint enforcement arrangements that expand the scope and enforceability of AI governance measures.

Stronger policy alignment among the US and regional partners leads to coordinated procurement rules, standards and exclusion of certain vendors, accelerating fragmentation between Western and Chinese technology ecosystems.

Tighter export controls legally block shipments of high-end accelerators, training hardware and specialized design tools, directly reducing the training throughput and peak scale of models available to affected developers.

When legal transfer channels are restricted, state and non‑state actors have stronger incentives to pursue illicit acquisition via cyberespionage and supply‑chain intrusion, raising successful attacks against AI infrastructure.

Tighter export controls on specialized refinery catalysts, control electronics and spare parts reduce import-dependent refineries' ability to maintain and replace critical components, causing measurable declines in processing rates as inventories of spares are exhausted.

Tightened US export controls on dual‑use maritime and aerospace technologies incentivize China to deepen security ties and expedite transfers of asymmetric maritime capabilities to partners like Iran, raising incidents of harassment, interdiction and risk to commercial shipping in Gulf sea lanes.

Tighter export controls on advanced semiconductors and sensors reduce availability of critical components that would otherwise be re-exported or procured for Russian guided munitions, drones and ISR systems, degrading Russia's ability to sustain high-tempo operations.

Greater fragmentation of standards and incompatible stacks forces firms to reengineer, certify, and localize models for multiple ecosystems, lengthening integration and rollout timelines and slowing deployment.

An increase in tech decoupling forces US-aligned states to adopt common standards, procurement and security-of-supply policies, which raises interoperability and formal coordination among allies responding to the conflict.

Intense domestic political pressure (from voters or industry constituencies) accelerates legislative and executive action to expand scope, enforcement powers and resourcing of AI oversight bodies, strengthening regulation.

Intense domestic political pressure can drive near-term policy actions (export bans, tariffs, or import restrictions) that remove supply from markets or increase transaction costs, producing upward pressure on liquid fuel prices.

Intensified domestic political pressure in the US to prioritize competition with China leads to redeployment of naval and air assets toward the Indo‑Pacific, weakening deterrence in the Gulf and encouraging Iran and its proxies to increase missile, rocket and armed‑drone strike activity.

A drop in US–China strategic trust reduces Beijing's willingness to coordinate high‑level deconfliction and back‑channel diplomacy with Washington over Iran, producing fewer joint or bilateral diplomatic interventions aimed at calming Gulf tensions.

Higher crude export flows increase revenue for oil-dependent states and defence budgets, enabling sustained or expanded funding for military AI safety R&D, testing, and engineering programs; conversely drops in exports tend to force cuts in those programs.

Higher crude export flows normalize tanker schedules and reduce the economic and strategic incentives for interdiction or rerouting, lowering the incidence and severity of maritime trade disruptions in the Gulf.

Larger crude export volumes increase export revenues and foreign‑currency liquidity available to a belligerent state, easing financing of ammunition procurement, energy purchases and sustainment, which in turn supports a higher sustained military operations intensity over time.

Sustained reductions in crude export volumes lower exporters' foreign-exchange earnings and shipping throughput, leading governments and logistics providers to prioritize energy shipments or barter deals and consequently reduce the volume of rare-earth and critical-mineral consignments along the bilateral corridor.

Higher refinery throughput increases availability of refined fuels (diesel, jet fuel) required for mechanized and air operations, enabling higher tempo and geographic reach of military operations, while throughput drops constrain fuel supply and reduce operational intensity.

Restored or increased pipeline transit stabilizes local power/fuel supplies for datacenters and on‑premise training facilities, allowing paused or curtailed large-scale model training and compute‑intensive development to resume, raising aggregate deployed model capability.
Increases in pipeline transit capacity/throughput shift volumes off sea routes, reducing tanker congestion and target density and thus lowering the risk and severity of maritime trade disruption.

Sustained decreases in pipeline transit most commonly reflect physical closures, damage or preemptive shut‑offs that directly cause outages, flow interruptions and cascading operational losses across connected energy infrastructure.

Higher levels of commercial fuel inventories reduce immediate supply anxiety among importers and exporters, decreasing the frequency and urgency of high-level diplomatic contacts and emergency negotiations over Gulf security.

A sharp drawdown in commercial and strategic fuel inventories prompts authorities to tighten legal and administrative export restrictions on energy-related goods and associated dual-use technologies to conserve supplies and prevent outward flows to strategic competitors such as China.

Sustained rises in liquid fuel prices raise operational costs for military platforms and logistics, incentivizing defence services and contractors to accelerate deployment of AI-driven optimization/autonomy (route planning, fuel-saving autonomy, logistics automation) to cut fuel consumption.

Sharp upward movements in fuel prices create political pressure and strategic urgency for governments to secure supply lines, prompting more intensive state-led protection, patrols, and retaliatory operations in the Gulf.

Sharp rises in fuel prices create shared economic and operational pressures that prompt coordinated allied policy responses (e.g., price caps, joint procurement, pooled logistics and releases from reserves) to stabilize supplies for the conflict theater.

Rapid rises in retail and industrial fuel prices increase inflation and visible economic pain for voters and firms, producing immediate domestic pressure on policymakers to adopt protectionist or security-first measures in trade and technology negotiations with China.

Prolonged high fuel prices raise the strategic priority of reducing external energy and supply-chain exposure, accelerating industrial policies (subsidies, localization mandates and selective restrictions) that deepen technological ecosystem fragmentation between the US and China.

Higher AI model capability improves autonomous targeting, sensor fusion and swarm coordination for loitering munitions and armed drones used by state and proxy actors, enabling more frequent and higher‑impact strike operations.
Higher AI model capability improves real‑time ISR, target discrimination and automated fire‑control, lowering decision and targeting times and enabling higher tempo and scale of kinetic operations.

A demonstrable jump in AI model capabilities (dual‑use performance) prompts policymakers to adopt targeted restrictions on cross‑border transfers of models, weights and high‑end compute because those assets are reclassified as strategically sensitive.

Rapid deployment of unvetted military AI (autonomous maritime/aerial interdiction systems and rushed targeting software) raises the incidence of operational interdictions or accidents at export terminals and tankers, reducing crude export flows.

Faster operational rollout of AI-enabled systems (autonomous drones, loitering munitions and remote targeting tools) increases the number of fielded platforms capable of conducting cross‑border strikes, raising incident frequency.

Rapid large‑scale deployment of advanced AI systems by one side increases incentives for firms and governments on the other side to accelerate creation of separate standards, supplier lists and incompatible stacks, raising overall technological decoupling.

Increased safety engineering applied to military and industrial AI controlling pipeline valves and supervisories reduces false trips, miscommands and software-induced shutdowns, improving pipeline reliability and transit rates.

Greater investment in safety engineering and testing for deployed aerial and maritime AI reduces false positives, loss-of-control events and emergent interactions that would otherwise cause accidental interdictions or blockages of shipping lanes.

When governments invest in and empower AI governance bodies they rapidly translate that authority into tighter legally enforceable export controls on sensitive models, chips and related tooling to manage national security risks.
Increased successful compromises of refinery industrial control systems (SCADA/ICS) cause emergency shutdowns, deratings or prolonged recovery work, directly lowering refinery throughput.

An increase in successful AI‑enabled cyber intrusions against military command-and-control, air-defence sensors or critical infrastructure in the Gulf leads affected states to attribute operational degradation to adversaries and to carry out kinetic retaliatory strikes to reassert deterrence.

An increased rate of successful cyberattacks exploiting AI systems and their toolchains enables adversaries to intrude into industrial control and dispatch systems, producing more frequent and severe outages of energy infrastructure.

A spike in successful AI‑enabled cyber intrusions against critical infrastructure and firms generates immediate public outcry and lobbying pressure on legislators and executives to pursue protectionist trade and tech measures.

Military operations intensity
nodes.description: Measures the overall scale, tempo and geographic extent of kinetic combat operations across the theatre of conflict.

nodes.label: Cross-border attack rate
nodes.description: Measures the frequency per unit time of strikes, drone attacks and other kinetic incidents that cross internationally recognized borders.

nodes.label: Energy infrastructure disruption
nodes.description: Measures the extent and duration of outages, damage and operational loss across energy production, refining and transmission infrastructure.

nodes.label: Corporate asset seizure activity
nodes.description: Measures the rate and scale of state-directed seizures, takeovers or administrative controls applied to foreign-owned commercial assets.

nodes.label: Sanctions and trade restriction severity
nodes.description: Measures the aggregate breadth and restrictiveness of economic sanctions, tariffs and trade controls applied in response to the conflict.

nodes.label: Arms transfer volume
nodes.description: Measures the flow rate and quantity of military equipment, munitions and support delivered to conflict parties or proximate actors.

nodes.label: Air‑defense capacity
nodes.description: Measures the deployed and operational capability of integrated air‑defense systems and intercept assets available in the theatre.

nodes.label: Cyber-attack activity level
nodes.description: Measures the frequency, scale and sophistication of offensive cyber operations targeting infrastructure, institutions or information environments related to the conflict.

nodes.label: Election interference activity
nodes.description: Measures the intensity and prevalence of actions aimed at influencing or disrupting electoral processes, including disinformation and technical interference.

nodes.label: Domestic repression intensity
nodes.description: Measures the level of political repression, civil liberties restrictions and punitive actions taken against dissent within affected jurisdictions.

nodes.label: Allied security coordination strength
nodes.description: Measures the degree of operational, intelligence and policy coordination among aligned actors responding to the conflict.

nodes.label: International legal and policy contestation
nodes.description: Measures the volume and intensity of disputes, litigation, sanctions debates and policy negotiations in international legal and multilateral fora related to the conflict.

nodes.label: Global energy market volatility
nodes.description: Measures price volatility, supply uncertainty and short‑term fluctuations in global energy markets attributable to the conflict and related measures.

nodes.label: Supply chain disruption level
nodes.description: Measures the extent of interruptions, delays and rerouting across critical export/import logistics and industrial supply chains linked to the conflict.

nodes.label: Financial market volatility
nodes.description: Measures fluctuations in asset prices, capital flows and risk premia in financial markets connected to the conflict and policy responses.

nodes.label: Refugee and displacement flow rate
nodes.description: Measures the flow rate of internally displaced persons and cross‑border refugee movements generated by conflict dynamics.

nodes.label: Energy price volatility

nodes.label: Maritime trade disruption

nodes.label: Investor risk perception

nodes.label: Diplomatic engagement intensity

nodes.label: Sanctions pressure level

nodes.label: Travel advisory level

nodes.label: Defence system effectiveness

nodes.label: Alliance cohesion strength

nodes.label: Global institutional pressure

nodes.label: Critical infrastructure damage

nodes.label: Civilian displacement flow

nodes.label: Corporate lobbying pressure

nodes.label: Financial market volatility

nodes.label: Currency pressure
nodes.description: Directional stress on exchange-rate valuations linked to capital flows and policy signals emanating from the bilateral relationship.

nodes.label: Supply-chain resilience
nodes.description: Robustness of industrial supply chains to disruption, including substitution capacity and time-to-recovery for key components.

nodes.label: Technology decoupling degree
nodes.description: Extent of fragmentation between competing technological ecosystems, standards and interoperable infrastructures.

nodes.label: Regulatory enforcement capacity
nodes.description: Administrative and operational capacity to implement and enforce trade measures, export controls and safety regulations.

nodes.label: Domestic political pressure
nodes.description: Intensity of domestic political constraints, lobbying and public mobilization pushing negotiators toward protectionist or accommodative stances.

nodes.label: Investor confidence
nodes.description: Level of market participants' confidence regarding future returns and policy stability tied to the bilateral interaction.

nodes.label: Negotiation concession flow
nodes.description: Rate at which policy concessions, tariff adjustments or market-access commitments are offered, modified or accepted during talks.

nodes.label: Strategic trust level

nodes.label: Crude export flow
nodes.description: Volume of crude oil crossing borders and loaded for international export per unit time.

nodes.label: Refinery throughput rate
nodes.description: Rate at which refineries receive feedstock and process it into refined liquid products.

nodes.label: Refining conversion capacity
nodes.description: Installed physical capacity to convert crude input into refined liquid fuels (maximum processing capability).

nodes.label: Pipeline transit flow rate
nodes.description: Volume per unit time transported through pipeline networks between production, storage and refineries.

nodes.label: Tanker shipping availability
nodes.description: Effective available tanker fleet and charter capacity able to carry crude and refined products internationally.

nodes.label: Fuel storage inventory level
nodes.description: Aggregate volume of commercial and terminal storage holding crude and refined products at a point in time.

nodes.label: Strategic reserve level
nodes.description: Volume of government-held strategic petroleum reserves available for release or drawdown.

nodes.label: Liquid fuel price level
nodes.description: Market price level for key refined fuels (e.g., diesel, gasoline, marine bunkers) as observed by market participants.

nodes.label: Freight rate level
nodes.description: Cost level for shipping liquid fuels (tanker freight and charter rates) that influences transport economics.

nodes.label: Aggregate fuel demand rate
nodes.description: Total consumption rate of liquid fuels across all end‑use sectors per unit time.

nodes.label: Sectoral demand distribution
nodes.description: Relative allocation and dynamic shifts of fuel consumption among transport, industrial, agricultural and marine sectors.

nodes.label: Infrastructure disruption rate
nodes.description: Rate and intensity of unplanned outages, attacks or maintenance events that reduce pipeline, refinery or shipping operations.

nodes.label: Investment flow into capacity
nodes.description: Rate of financial investment directed toward upstream production, refining, storage and shipping capacity expansion or repair.

nodes.label: Policy restriction intensity
nodes.description: Degree and scope of trade measures, export controls, subsidies and regulatory interventions affecting fuel production and flows.

nodes.label: Geopolitical tension intensity
nodes.description: Overall level of geopolitical conflict, sanctions and diplomatic strain that influences cross‑border energy flows and risks.

Model capability level
nodes.description: The aggregate technical competence and functional performance of deployed AI models measured on a continuous scale of capability and complexity.

nodes.label: Deployment rate
nodes.description: The speed at which new or updated AI models and services are moved from development into real‑world operation.

nodes.label: Compute capacity
nodes.description: The available computational resources (hardware and provisioning) that can be allocated to AI training and inference at any time.

nodes.label: Capital investment rate
nodes.description: The flow of financial resources being directed into AI development, infrastructure and commercialization per unit time.

nodes.label: Commercialization pressure
nodes.description: The market and competitive incentives pushing actors to prioritize rapid productization and revenue generation from AI capabilities.

nodes.label: Safety engineering effort
nodes.description: The cumulative rate of work, resources and projects devoted to designing, testing and hardening AI systems for safety.

nodes.label: Independent evaluation capacity
nodes.description: The scale and readiness of non‑developer evaluative capabilities able to audit, test and certify AI systems independently.

nodes.label: Regulatory strength
nodes.description: The scope, enforceability and resourcing of rules and oversight mechanisms governing AI development and deployment.

nodes.label: Policy urgency level
nodes.description: The perceived immediacy and intensity of political and policy prioritization to act on AI‑related risks.

nodes.label: Cyberattack frequency
nodes.description: The rate at which adversarial actors successfully exploit, compromise or co‑opt AI systems or their infrastructure.

nodes.label: Misuse rate
nodes.description: The rate at which AI capabilities are repurposed for harmful, illegal, or unintended applications by users or adversaries.

nodes.label: Transparency level
nodes.description: The degree to which model architectures, training data provenance, evaluation results and risk assessments are disclosed and accessible.

nodes.label: Public trust level
nodes.description: The general population's confidence in AI systems and in the institutions governing their safety and use.

nodes.label: International coordination
nodes.description: The extent and effectiveness of cross‑jurisdictional alignment, information‑sharing and cooperative governance of AI.

nodes.label: Data access flow
nodes.description: The rate and volume at which data (training, validation, operational) is shared, transferred or made available for AI development.

nodes.label: Talent supply
nodes.description: The available pool and throughput of skilled personnel (researchers, engineers, safety specialists) for AI activities.

A drop in US–China strategic trust reduces Beijing's willingness to coordinate high‑level deconfliction and back‑channel diplomacy with Washington over Iran, producing fewer joint or bilateral diplomatic interventions aimed at calming Gulf tensions.

Higher crude export flows increase revenue for oil-dependent states and defence budgets, enabling sustained or expanded funding for military AI safety R&D, testing, and engineering programs; conversely drops in exports tend to force cuts in those programs.

Higher crude export flows normalize tanker schedules and reduce the economic and strategic incentives for interdiction or rerouting, lowering the incidence and severity of maritime trade disruptions in the Gulf.

Larger crude export volumes increase export revenues and foreign‑currency liquidity available to a belligerent state, easing financing of ammunition procurement, energy purchases and sustainment, which in turn supports a higher sustained military operations intensity over time.

Sustained reductions in crude export volumes lower exporters' foreign-exchange earnings and shipping throughput, leading governments and logistics providers to prioritize energy shipments or barter deals and consequently reduce the volume of rare-earth and critical-mineral consignments along the bilateral corridor.

Higher refinery throughput increases availability of refined fuels (diesel, jet fuel) required for mechanized and air operations, enabling higher tempo and geographic reach of military operations, while throughput drops constrain fuel supply and reduce operational intensity.

Restored or increased pipeline transit stabilizes local power/fuel supplies for datacenters and on‑premise training facilities, allowing paused or curtailed large-scale model training and compute‑intensive development to resume, raising aggregate deployed model capability.
Increases in pipeline transit capacity/throughput shift volumes off sea routes, reducing tanker congestion and target density and thus lowering the risk and severity of maritime trade disruption.

Sustained decreases in pipeline transit most commonly reflect physical closures, damage or preemptive shut‑offs that directly cause outages, flow interruptions and cascading operational losses across connected energy infrastructure.

Higher levels of commercial fuel inventories reduce immediate supply anxiety among importers and exporters, decreasing the frequency and urgency of high-level diplomatic contacts and emergency negotiations over Gulf security.

A sharp drawdown in commercial and strategic fuel inventories prompts authorities to tighten legal and administrative export restrictions on energy-related goods and associated dual-use technologies to conserve supplies and prevent outward flows to strategic competitors such as China.

Sustained rises in liquid fuel prices raise operational costs for military platforms and logistics, incentivizing defence services and contractors to accelerate deployment of AI-driven optimization/autonomy (route planning, fuel-saving autonomy, logistics automation) to cut fuel consumption.

Sharp upward movements in fuel prices create political pressure and strategic urgency for governments to secure supply lines, prompting more intensive state-led protection, patrols, and retaliatory operations in the Gulf.

Sharp rises in fuel prices create shared economic and operational pressures that prompt coordinated allied policy responses (e.g., price caps, joint procurement, pooled logistics and releases from reserves) to stabilize supplies for the conflict theater.

Rapid rises in retail and industrial fuel prices increase inflation and visible economic pain for voters and firms, producing immediate domestic pressure on policymakers to adopt protectionist or security-first measures in trade and technology negotiations with China.

Prolonged high fuel prices raise the strategic priority of reducing external energy and supply-chain exposure, accelerating industrial policies (subsidies, localization mandates and selective restrictions) that deepen technological ecosystem fragmentation between the US and China.

Higher AI model capability improves autonomous targeting, sensor fusion and swarm coordination for loitering munitions and armed drones used by state and proxy actors, enabling more frequent and higher‑impact strike operations.
Higher AI model capability improves real‑time ISR, target discrimination and automated fire‑control, lowering decision and targeting times and enabling higher tempo and scale of kinetic operations.

A demonstrable jump in AI model capabilities (dual‑use performance) prompts policymakers to adopt targeted restrictions on cross‑border transfers of models, weights and high‑end compute because those assets are reclassified as strategically sensitive.

Rapid deployment of unvetted military AI (autonomous maritime/aerial interdiction systems and rushed targeting software) raises the incidence of operational interdictions or accidents at export terminals and tankers, reducing crude export flows.

Faster operational rollout of AI-enabled systems (autonomous drones, loitering munitions and remote targeting tools) increases the number of fielded platforms capable of conducting cross‑border strikes, raising incident frequency.

Rapid large‑scale deployment of advanced AI systems by one side increases incentives for firms and governments on the other side to accelerate creation of separate standards, supplier lists and incompatible stacks, raising overall technological decoupling.

Increased safety engineering applied to military and industrial AI controlling pipeline valves and supervisories reduces false trips, miscommands and software-induced shutdowns, improving pipeline reliability and transit rates.

Greater investment in safety engineering and testing for deployed aerial and maritime AI reduces false positives, loss-of-control events and emergent interactions that would otherwise cause accidental interdictions or blockages of shipping lanes.

When governments invest in and empower AI governance bodies they rapidly translate that authority into tighter legally enforceable export controls on sensitive models, chips and related tooling to manage national security risks.
Increased successful compromises of refinery industrial control systems (SCADA/ICS) cause emergency shutdowns, deratings or prolonged recovery work, directly lowering refinery throughput.

An increase in successful AI‑enabled cyber intrusions against military command-and-control, air-defence sensors or critical infrastructure in the Gulf leads affected states to attribute operational degradation to adversaries and to carry out kinetic retaliatory strikes to reassert deterrence.

An increased rate of successful cyberattacks exploiting AI systems and their toolchains enables adversaries to intrude into industrial control and dispatch systems, producing more frequent and severe outages of energy infrastructure.

A spike in successful AI‑enabled cyber intrusions against critical infrastructure and firms generates immediate public outcry and lobbying pressure on legislators and executives to pursue protectionist trade and tech measures.
